problem: End-to-end RGB-only DRL agents for zero-shot object-goal navigation degrade when transferred directly to real robots, because of appearance gaps between simulated and real objects and because real cameras have a much narrower FoV than the wide-angle views in AI2-THOR. Attention-based methods such as TDANet also focus on a few target-like objects and discard useful scene context.
motivation: Real environments contain countless object categories, so knowledge graphs or absolute object recognition do not scale to unseen classes. Comparing a novel object against familiar ones (difference-based learning) should give more domain-independent features. A narrow FoV makes targets vanish during rotation, so short-term memory is needed.
key_idea: Compute Siamese element-wise absolute differences between target and every detected object embedding, mean-pool them into a scene feature, and feed a two-frame temporal buffer to an LSTM actor-critic to handle narrow FoV and unseen classes.
insight: Aggregating differences over all detected objects beats Top-k selection of target-like objects (SR 62.7 vs 22.8-39.2 on the 14/8 split), so context objects act as spatial anchors. In the real-world ablation the difference module gives most of the gain (SR 7.7 -> 51.3) and the temporal buffer adds more (-> 64.1). Longer history hurts (10-step SR 54.1 vs 2-step 71.9), suggesting that noise accumulates under restricted FoV.
method: Object features: each detected object is a 303-d vector [x, y, area, 300-d GloVe label embedding]; the target is encoded the same way (detections from YOLOv7 in real-world tests).
Siamese difference extractor: a shared projection (linear+ReLU, then W_L) maps target and object, takes |W_L X_ri - W_L X_t|, then applies FFN + residual + LayerNorm to give V_di.
Scene aggregation: mean-pool V_di over all n detected objects to handle a variable object count.
Dual-frame temporal buffer: keep scene features of t-1 and t, concatenate each with the embedded previous action (E_t in R^{2x522}), and feed the pair to an LSTM.
A3C actor-critic heads on the LSTM hidden state.
Reward: +5 for Done with target visible, plus a partial reward R_p = R_t*Pr(t|p)*0.1 the first time a parent object is seen (MJOLNIR prior), -0.01 per step.
Deployment: policy trained in AI2-THOR is deployed unchanged on a TurtleBot4 via ROS2 with discrete actions (MoveAhead 0.25 m, Rotate 45°, LookUp/Down 30°, Done).

setting.backbone: Custom lightweight Siamese difference network + LSTM actor-critic (A3C), trained from scratch; GloVe embeddings; YOLOv7 detector
setting.training_data: AI2-THOR v1.0.1 offline data, 6,000,000 episodes, 20 training rooms per scene type (kitchen, living room, bedroom, bathroom), 22 object classes split into seen/unseen
setting.observation: egocentric monocular RGB (converted to detected boxes + labels)
setting.action_space: discrete: MoveAhead 0.25 m, RotateLeft/Right 45°, LookUp/Down 30°, Done
setting.privileged: none at test time (the parent-object prior is used only for the training reward)

results: T-DRN reaches SR 71.9 (L>=1) and 57.2 (L>=5) on the 18/4 split, versus TDANet's 62.5 and 47.7. On the 14/8 split it reaches SR 62.7 and 42.7 versus TDANet's 53.4 and 41.2, and SPL is about equal to TDANet. On a real TurtleBot4 it reaches SR 64.1 versus 53.8 for TDANet and 20.5 for MJOLNIR, with 2.96M parameters and 0.5 ms latency.
limitations: RGB-only, no depth, so obstacle proximity is misjudged and collisions cause failures.
The real-world evaluation is small (39 trials, three rooms) and depends on a YOLOv7 detector; the simulation protocol is a nonstandard AI2-THOR split and covers only 22 classes.
Memory covers only two frames, so multi-room and long-horizon navigation is not addressed.
